title: One feature flips the verdict
outcomes: Predicts how one changed feature (a neighbouring pawn, an extra defender) flips a pawn verdict
Fixes a backward pawn first, then counts attackers against defenders
Says which check a change breaks: fixed, reachable or counted

steps.text: In the last lesson (*Weak, harmless or compensated: rating a pawn*) you asked: can it advance, can my pieces reach it, does anything pay for it? Today the first two become *fixed* and *reachable*, and you add *counted*: attackers against defenders. A verdict can flip when **one feature** changes: a neighbouring pawn arrives, a defender is added, a file closes. Predict the flip before you look. Open files and the bishop pair flip verdicts too; they have their own lessons.

steps.title: Isolated or not?
steps.prompt: Only one pawn has moved. Predict whether the white b-pawn is still isolated, then check.

steps.title: Backward or not?
steps.prompt: Only one pawn has moved. Predict whether the black a-pawn is still backward, then check.

steps.text: To win a backward pawn, work in two steps. **Fix it:** check that the square in front of it is attacked by a pawn, so it cannot run. **Then count:** attackers against defenders, with the king counting as a defender. As a *rule of thumb*, you need more attackers than it has defenders, and no exchange may cost you more counting value than you take.

steps.title: Fixed, then counted
steps.prompt: Only the black king has moved, from g8 to f7. Predict whether Rxe6 still wins a pawn.

steps.text: A fixed pawn is not automatically lost. An extra defender, even the king, can turn a win into nothing, and a neighbour that can still protect the pawn means it is not backward at all. For each change, ask which check it breaks: **fixed**, **reachable** or **counted**.

steps.prompt: Before you looked, how sure were you which feature would flip the verdict? Which of the three checks did the change break? (low / medium / high)
